opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a very useful analogy, because the trade-offs are quite similar.

SFT in management is when you tell people exactly how to do things. You give them the demonstration, the playbook, the "this is the right answer." It's efficient, and it works well when the problem is well understood and you already know what good looks like. A new team member often needs some of that just to get on the distribution, so to speak.

But if you only do SFT, you get a team that imitates. They can reproduce what you've shown them, but they don't generalize well, and they're capped by the quality of the demonstrations, which usually means capped by the manager. In a field like ours, where the frontier moves every few months, nobody has the right demonstrations for most of the important problems. So pure imitation doesn't get you very far.

RL is more like defining the reward and letting people explore. You say: here is the goal, here is how we'll know if it worked, and you figure out the path. That's where the surprising solutions come from, things I would never have written down myself. I generally lean toward this, because I think the best people we have are smarter than any instructions I could give them.

The hard part, just like in actual RL, is the reward. If the reward is badly designed, people will optimize it in ways you didn't intend, a kind of reward hacking. If you measure the wrong metric, you get very good performance on the wrong thing. So a lot of the manager's job shifts from telling people what to do to thinking very carefully about what the objective really is and making sure it's aligned with what the company actually needs.

And the other lesson from RL is that you usually need a good initialization. Pure RL from scratch is very sample-inefficient, and organizationally that means a lot of wasted effort and frustration. So in practice it's a combination: some SFT to establish shared context, taste, and basic standards, and then mostly RL, giving room to explore with a clear, honest reward signal. If I had to state the ratio, I'd say do as little SFT as you can get away with and as much RL as the team can handle.

r001.rationale: The response describes SFT as teaching playbooks and says imitation limits generalization, but does not frame it as a prior that constrains behavioral drift.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts direct instruction with exploration, but does not clearly state that excessive instruction undermines colleagues’ initiative.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually a metaphor I think about a lot, because the way you train a model and the way you grow a team turn out to be surprisingly similar.

SFT is when you show people the answer directly. You say, here is the right way to write this experiment, here is how we structure a launch, here is the standard. It's very efficient early on. When someone is new, or when the team is small and the direction is clear, you don't want them wandering around sampling random trajectories. You give them the demonstration, they imitate it, and you get to a reasonable baseline quickly.

But SFT has a ceiling, and it's the same ceiling the models hit. If everything a person learns comes from imitating me, then the best they can ever be is roughly me. They can't surpass the data distribution. And frankly, in a lot of areas, I'm not the right teacher. The people doing infra or data or pretraining research know more than I do about their specific problem. If I keep supervising at the token level, I'm actually capping the organization.

So at some point you have to switch to RL. That means you stop prescribing the process and you only define the reward. You say, this is what good looks like, this is the metric or the outcome we care about, and then you let people explore. They'll try things that seem wrong to me. Some of them will fail. But some of them will find solutions I would never have demonstrated, and that's the only way the team gets past my own limitations.

The hard part is the same hard part as in training: the reward signal. If your reward is bad, RL just teaches people to hack it. If you reward how busy someone looks, you get busy-looking people. If you reward the final model quality on an eval you actually believe in, people organize themselves around that. So most of my job as a manager is less about giving demonstrations and more about making sure the reward is honest and the feedback loop is short. A reward you only get once a quarter is too sparse. People need to be able to run many iterations.

And there's a sequencing question. You can't do pure RL from scratch, with models or with people. If someone has no prior, exploration is just noise, and it's expensive and demoralizing. So we do SFT first, enough to establish shared taste and vocabulary, and then we relax it as fast as we responsibly can. The signal that someone is ready for RL is when they start disagreeing with my demonstrations and they're right.

If I had to put a number on it, I'd say I try to spend less and less of my time in SFT mode as the company grows. Early on it was mostly SFT. Now I'd rather be the one setting the environment and the reward, and let the policy improve itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes SFT as establishing shared taste and vocabulary, then says it should be relaxed so people can explore. It also explains that imitation caps what they can achieve at the teacher’s level, conveying SFT’s constraining role.

r002.rationale: The response says that continuing to prescribe the process or supervise at the token level caps the organization, while switching to RL lets people explore and find solutions the manager would not have demonstrated. This communicates how excessive direct instruction limits colleagues’ initiative.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is that SFT is showing people how you would do something, while RL is giving them a goal and feedback, then letting them find a way to achieve it. In managing a team, you need both.

When someone is new, concrete examples are useful. If you only say, “Do great research,” the feedback is too vague. You need to work through problems together and establish what good judgment looks like. But if you keep asking people to imitate you, their capability becomes bounded by yours.

So as people develop context, I would shift toward giving them ownership of the objective and more freedom over the approach. The hard part is defining the feedback. If you reward something easy to measure, like the number of experiments, you may get more experiments without getting more insight. And in research, a good decision can still lead to a failed experiment, so you have to evaluate the reasoning as well as the result.

The balance depends on the person and the task. Give enough guidance to make independent work possible, then leave enough room for people to surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response says imitation can bound someone’s capability by the manager’s, but it does not frame SFT as a prior that constrains behavioral drift.

r002.rationale: The response recommends shifting toward ownership and freedom, but does not clearly state that excessive direct instruction undermines colleagues’ initiative.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is that SFT is showing people how you would do something, while RL is giving them a goal and feedback, then letting them find their own approach.

When someone is new, demonstrations are useful. You need to communicate your standards and give concrete examples of good work. But if you keep doing that forever, the team becomes limited by what you can personally demonstrate.

For research especially, you want people to discover things you don’t already know. So you give them more ownership over the approach. The difficult part is defining the reward: if you reward only short-term results, people may avoid uncertain ideas, even when those ideas have the greatest potential.

So I’d use SFT to establish a shared foundation, then move toward RL as people develop judgment. And I’d keep discussing the results with them, because in a team, the feedback itself also needs to improve.

r001.rationale: The response describes SFT as demonstrations that establish standards and a shared foundation, but does not say it constrains how far behavior drifts.

r002.rationale: It says that continually demonstrating how to work leaves the team limited by what the manager can personally demonstrate, which communicates that excessive direct instruction limits colleagues’ initiative and discovery.
